notes.meaning: The people of Ziph come to King Saul at Gibeah to tell him where David is hiding. Saul had recently promised to leave David alone, but the Ziphites stir up his jealousy once more. Their report pulls Saul right back into his old hunt.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view chapter 26 and chapter 24 as two different tellings of the exact same event passed down through different oral traditions.

notes.meaning: Saul takes three thousand picked soldiers down to the desert of Ziph to hunt for David. Even though he had wept and admitted his wrong before, his good feelings quickly fade. He returns to his old sin instead of keeping his word.

Saul sets up camp along the road near the hill of Hachilah. David stays out in the wild areas and learns that Saul has marched out after him. Instead of rushing out to fight, David chooses to stay hidden and keep watch.

David sends out scouts to make sure Saul has truly arrived. He does not rely on rumors alone, but gathers solid facts before making any move. This careful scouting lets David act wisely without putting his men in needless danger.

David creeps close to Saul's camp to see how the army is arranged. Saul is sleeping in the center of the camp inside a circle formed by his wagons and troops, with his general Abner nearby. David shows great personal bravery by going to scout the camp with his own eyes.

David asks two of his men who is willing to sneak into Saul's camp with him. Ahimelech says nothing, but David's nephew Abishai boldly volunteers to go. David trusts God to protect them on this dangerous nighttime mission.

David and Abishai slip quietly into the camp in the middle of the night. Saul is fast asleep with his royal spear pushed into the ground right by his head, and his whole army is sleeping around him. God leaves the king completely exposed and helpless before the man he is hunting.

Abishai whispers to David that God has handed his enemy over to him. He asks for permission to pin Saul to the ground with one strike of the spear, promising he will not need a second blow. Abishai assumes that having the opportunity to kill Saul means God wants them to do it.

David refuses to let Abishai kill the king. Saul was "the Lord's anointed," meaning God had chosen him and set him apart with holy oil to rule Israel. David knows that anyone who harms God's chosen king will bear heavy guilt.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some teachers use David's words about not touching God's anointed to claim that church members should never question, challenge, or correct their leaders.

notes.meaning: David tells Abishai that God Himself will deal with Saul. Saul will either be struck down by God, die of old age, or fall in battle against Israel's enemies. David chooses to wait for God's timing instead of forcing his own way to the throne.

David declares that he will never lift his hand against the Lord's anointed king. Instead, he tells Abishai to take Saul's spear and the water jug near his head so they can leave. These two items would prove they had been right beside the sleeping king without harming him.

David takes the spear and water jug from beside Saul's head, and the two men leave safely. Not a single guard wakes up or sees them because the Lord had put everyone into a deep, supernatural sleep. God was watching over David and keeping him safe every step of the way.

David climbs to the top of a hill across the valley, putting a wide space between himself and Saul's camp. He makes sure he is safe from an attack while still being close enough to be heard. The open mountain air allows his voice to carry across the deep ravine.

David shouts out to the sleeping soldiers and calls directly to Abner, the commander of Saul's army. Abner wakes up and asks who is yelling and disturbing the king. David uses this moment to hold the general accountable for failing to guard his master.

David mocks Abner by asking why such a famous warrior failed to protect his master. He explains that an intruder had entered the camp with the power to kill the king. Abner was known for his courage, but he had fallen asleep on guard duty.

David tells Abner that his failure is so serious that he deserves to die under military law for leaving God's anointed king unguarded. To prove it, David tells him to look around for the king's spear and water jug. This evidence shows that David was the one who actually protected Saul's life.

Saul wakes up, recognizes David's voice, and calls out affectionately to him as his son. David answers with deep respect, calling Saul his lord and king. Even while being hunted as a rebel, David treats the king with great honor.

David asks Saul why he keeps chasing someone who wants only to serve him. He asks what crime he has committed or what evil is found in his hands. David appeals to the facts, knowing his conscience is completely clean.

David suggests two possible reasons for Saul's chase. If God stirred Saul up, they should offer a sacrifice, a worship gift to restore peace with God; but if evil men urged Saul on, they are cursed. By driving David out of Israel, those men were practically forcing him away from God's worship to live among idolaters.

David begs Saul not to spill his blood in a foreign land far away from God's sanctuary. He points out how foolish it is for the king of Israel to lead an army just to hunt a tiny flea or chase a partridge in the hills. Hunting down a harmless servant brings shame rather than honor to a king.

Saul breaks down and confesses that he has sinned, inviting David to come home. He admits that he has acted like a fool and made a terrible mistake because David treated his life as precious. Yet Saul's remorse was only temporary, without real spiritual change toward God.

David tells Saul to send a young soldier over to retrieve the royal spear. By giving the spear back, David shows that he has no desire to seize Saul's throne by violence. He returns the weapon as physical proof of his pure motives.

David declares that the Lord rewards every person who walks in righteousness and faithfulness. God gave Saul into David's hands that night, but David refused to strike the Lord's anointed king. David looks to God rather than to Saul to judge his actions and reward his loyalty.

David prays that just as he valued Saul's life, the Lord will value his life and rescue him from all trouble. He puts his future safety in God's hands rather than relying on Saul's promises. David knows that true safety comes only from the Lord.

Saul blesses David and admits that David will accomplish great things and surely succeed. After this, David goes his own way and Saul returns home, and the two men never see each other again. David wisely keeps his distance because he knows Saul's promises cannot be trusted.
